summary: Discusses considerations for assigning a new recommended DSCP for a standard PHB, including how Diffserv markings are commonly re-marked along Internet paths and implications of using a particular code point.

eli5.summary: Packets get priority labels, but along the way the labels may be changed. This asks what to think about before adding a new one.

questions: how to choose a diffserv code point
how to assign a new dscp
subtitle: How to choose a good Differentiated Services Code Point when assigning a new one.

tldr.problem: When the IETF considers assigning a new DSCP for a standard Per-Hop Behavior, decision-makers need guidance on how DSCP values behave across the Internet, since various networks re-mark or bleach the DSCP field in unpredictable ways.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9435 documents observed re-marking behaviors (bleaching, precedence manipulation, lower-layer mappings) and provides considerations for selecting a new DSCP value that will remain meaningful end-to-end despite these transformations.
tldr.outcome: New DSCP assignments are made with awareness of Internet re-marking patterns, improving the likelihood that the intended QoS treatment survives across diverse network paths.

today: RFC 9435 is an Informational RFC published in July 2023 and has not been obsoleted. It provides guidance to the IETF and IESG for considering new DSCP assignments. IANA has added a note to the DSCP registry referencing this RFC for considerations when assigning a new codepoint.

sections.title: The DSCP Problem
sections.content: The Diffserv architecture allows networks to mark IP packets with a 6-bit DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) to indicate the Per-Hop Behavior (PHB) each router should apply—determining priority, queuing, and drop probability. The IETF has assigned specific recommended DSCPs to various PHBs. However, observations across Internet paths show that many networks re-mark the DSCP field, either intentionally or as a side effect of older equipment, lower-layer QoS implementations, or security policies. A DSCP that is carefully chosen for one standard may be inadvertently transformed as the packet traverses the Internet, losing the intended treatment. The IETF and IESG need guidance when considering new DSCP assignments to avoid these pitfalls.
sections.eli5: Packets get labels that say how important they are, but lots of routers along the way might change those labels or ignore them. We need to pick new labels that survive the changes.

sections.title: Common DSCP Re-marking Behaviors
sections.content: Measurements of Internet paths reveal seven observed re-marking behaviors. Bleach-DSCP sets all traffic to zero (Best Effort). Bleach-ToS-Precedence resets the first three bits to zero, a behavior stemming from older Type of Service semantics predating Diffserv. Bleach-some-ToS is similar but preserves traffic marked with the two highest bits set (DSCPs 0b11xxxx). Re-mark-ToS sets the first three bits to a specific value other than zero. Bleach-low and Bleach-some-low reset the last three bits to zero. Re-mark-DSCP re-marks traffic to one or more specific DSCP values, often as part of traffic conditioning. These behaviors occur at network edges, in old equipment, in MPLS domains, in mobile networks, in carrier Ethernet, and in lower-layer systems that map DSCP to 3-bit priority fields.
sections.eli5: Some routers erase all labels and set everything to normal. Some erase just part of the label. Some change it to a specific number. And some do this only for certain traffic.

sections.title: Lower-Layer Mapping and Interactions
sections.content: Systems below the IP layer also interact with DSCP. IEEE 802.1Q Ethernet maps the first three bits of the DSCP to a 3-bit Priority Code Point (PCP). IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi maps DSCP to a 3-bit User Priority (UP) in multiple ways: some equipment maps the first three bits, some maps the entire DSCP by shifting, and access points may re-mark according to QoS profiles. MPLS networks use 3-bit Traffic Classes and employ three models (Pipe, Short Pipe, Uniform) with different DSCP handling at domain boundaries. Mobile networks (LTE, 5G) map DSCP to QoS Class Identifiers. Carrier Ethernet providers also perform DSCP to L2 QoS mappings. Additionally, other policies may re-mark DSCP as a side effect of DDoS mitigation or other functions. Understanding these interactions is essential when selecting a new DSCP to ensure it survives end-to-end traversal.
sections.eli5: Different networks use different number of bits for priority. Some take only part of your label and convert it to their system, and when your packet leaves, the number might be different.

sections.title: Selecting a New DSCP
sections.content: RFC 9435 provides guidance for DSCP selection. For a new DSCP greater than 7, consider what happens when ToS Precedence is bleached (the first three bits are cleared), as this is common. DSCPs with values 0bxxx001 (ending in 1) are particularly risky: if bleached, they become DSCP 1 (Lower Effort), which could invert traffic priority. For DSCPs less than or equal to 7, consider that ToS Precedence Bleaching may aggregate multiple assigned DSCPs (e.g., AF11, AF21, AF31, AF41 would all become DSCP 2), increasing contention. New assignments should also consider impact on deployed infrastructure and how treatment aggregation and lower-layer mappings affect the proposed DSCP. The assignment process should be informed by these considerations and should consider whether an existing DSCP already serves the need, whether the request uses Pools 1, 2, or 3, and what the implications are for operators and interoperability.
sections.eli5: If you pick a label with certain numbers, and someone bleaches the first part, you might get a different treatment than intended. Some numbers are safer than others.

sections.title: Implications for Interoperability
sections.content: A new DSCP assignment is only effective if it provides the intended treatment end-to-end. However, networks that do not implement Diffserv, networks that bleach or re-mark aggressively, and networks that map DSCP to lower-layer priorities all transform the DSCP value. An operator cannot rely on the recommended DSCP surviving unchanged. The RFC notes that new DSCP assignments should consider the most common re-marking patterns observed across the Internet and should be designed to remain meaningful even if bleached or transformed. For example, a DSCP that remains identifiable by its lower three bits after bleaching of the first three bits is more robust. The goal is not to guarantee that the DSCP never changes—that is impossible—but to choose a value that degrades gracefully when transformed.
sections.eli5: You can't promise your label will never be changed, but you can pick one that still works okay if it gets changed in common ways.
